headline: Federal scholarship for private school and homeschooling opening to most kids in at least 30 states
summary: The Trump administration has proposed a new federal scholarship program starting Jan. 1, 2023, allowing nearly all schoolchildren in at least 30 states to apply for taxpayer-funded incentives for private or homeschooling expenses. Public school students can also use funds for tutoring or therapies. About 96% of children in participating states are eligible, with simplified income verification for low-income families. The program could direct nearly $26 billion into approximately 2.2 million scholarships annually once fully operational. Governors have mixed reactions, with some seeing opportunities for student support while others worry about resource diversion from public schools.

headline: Can Vermont afford Proposal 3?
summary: Vermont's population decline and economic stagnation are attributed to union power. Proposal 3, if passed, could exacerbate these issues by locking in union privileges, potentially leading to job losses, reduced investment, and higher taxes. This could strain Vermont's state budget, with property taxpayers likely footing the bill.

headline: Republican voters split with party on gun law; Dems want more access to public records from Democrat-dominated offices
summary: Massachusetts voters seem divided along party lines on most ballot questions, but there are notable exceptions: many Republicans support keeping a 2024 gun law, and Democrats back applying public records law to the Legislature. A MassINC Polling Group survey showed 55% of Republicans favor retaining the gun law, while 61% of Democrats support making lawmakers subject to public records law, which the Legislature has resisted.

headline: Feds provide guidance on new federal K-12 scholarship tax credit program
summary: The federal Education Freedom Tax Credit program, starting in January, allows individuals to claim tax credits of up to $1,700 for donations to scholarship-granting organizations, primarily funding private school tuition but also covering public school expenses. So far, 30 states have opted into the program, with some governors facing political disputes over the decision. The program could result in up to 600 scholarship-granting organizations and nearly $26 billion in annual contributions by 2030.

headline: Voters to weigh different approaches to housing affordability in November
summary: Voters in four states will decide housing-related ballot measures in November, with California's Proposition 45 shortening environmental reviews, and Rhode Island's bond issue authorizing $120 million for affordable housing. Massachusetts' ballot measure aims to increase single-family home construction, while Hawaii's constitutional amendment could unlock housing development through special bonds. These measures could influence public opinion on housing policies and affordability.

headline: Republican attacks on the Missouri Supreme Court may just be the beginning
summary: Missouri Republicans, led by Secretary of State Denny Hoskins and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, engaged in a series of legal maneuvers challenging the Missouri Supreme Court's rulings on election maps, ultimately leading to public criticism of the court and threats of judicial impeachment.

headline: Nursing Nashville mom reunited with kids 3 months after ICE arrest
summary: ICE separated a nursing mother from her infant and toddler in Nashville, violating its own policy against detaining nursing parents under "exceptional circumstances." The mother was detained for nearly three months before being released. Human rights groups have accused ICE of routinely flouting its policies regarding pregnant, postpartum, and nursing mothers.

headline: In our re-segregated K-12 education system, Black parents face impossible choices
summary: Black parents face difficult decisions regarding school choice due to racial segregation and funding disparities, impacting their children's education and well-being.

headline: Judge rules Salah Sarsour is deportable
summary: A federal immigration judge ruled that Salah Sarsour, a vocal Palestinian rights advocate, can be deported, despite his attorneys' arguments that he was tortured in Israel and his actions do not undermine U.S. foreign policy. The ruling may be appealed to the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals.

headline: The numbers are in: EVs keep picking up steam in CT
summary: Connecticut's EV registrations reached 75,210 by July 2026, indicating growing public preference for electric vehicles despite political headwinds.

headline: Slotkin, bipartisan group of lawmakers introduce bill to improve ovarian cancer prevention and care
summary: Senator Elissa Slotkin introduced bipartisan legislation to expand access to ovarian cancer prevention and care, particularly in rural areas, aiming to improve early detection and survival rates. The bill, co-sponsored by Sen. Katie Britt and supported by the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, seeks to enhance genetic counseling, testing, and specialized care, with a focus on rural and underserved communities. If enacted, this policy could significantly improve public health outcomes for women at risk of ovarian cancer.

headline: Pennsylvania reports fifth measles-related death
summary: Pennsylvania has seen a fifth measles-related death this year, with 943 cases confirmed across 39 counties. The highly contagious virus has primarily affected unvaccinated individuals. The Pennsylvania Department of Health encourages vaccination as the best protection, offering the MMR vaccine at its 59 state health centers. Measles can cause serious health complications, including pneumonia and brain swelling.

headline: Georgia voters see tough future for next generation ahead of midterm race, poll finds
summary: A poll found that 70% of Georgians are pessimistic about children's prospects, with 68% citing expensive childcare. 63% would support a candidate advocating for affordable childcare and preschool. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms prioritized expanding pre-K access and proposed funding sources, while Republican candidate Rick Jackson pledged to improve child-related services without specifying details.
